edits.find: modern WordPress installations require PHP 8.2 or greater, MySQL 8.0 or MariaDB 10.5+, and HTTPS support. Hosts running outdated PHP runtimes or restrictive execution memory caps (e.g., 64MB or 128MB) will bottleneck complex site builds.
edits.replace: WordPress currently recommends PHP 8.3 or greater, MySQL 8.4 or greater or MariaDB 10.11 or greater, and HTTPS support. Hosts running outdated PHP versions or restrictive PHP memory limits can bottleneck complex site builds.
edits.reason: Outdated requirements; verified on wordpress.org (Nov 2026)

edits.find: Hostinger has established itself as an industry benchmark in the budget-to-midrange category by modernizing its server fleet with LiteSpeed Web Server Enterprise and high-throughput NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) SSD drives.
edits.replace: Hostinger's WordPress plans run on LiteSpeed servers, and most of its WordPress plans list NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) storage.
edits.reason: Removed hype; aligned with vendor page

edits.find: LSCache communicates directly with the web server kernel, bypassing PHP execution entirely for cached pages. This architecture enables entry-tier accounts to achieve sub-300ms static TTFB in independent network evaluations. Their custom-built hPanel interface provides clean access to PHP version toggles, object caching (available on higher tiers), and Cloudflare integration without the bloat of legacy cPanel skins.
edits.replace: LSCache works with the LiteSpeed server's built-in cache, so cached pages can be served without running PHP. Hostinger uses its own hPanel control panel rather than cPanel.
edits.reason: Removed unsourced sub-300ms TTFB claim and unverified plan details

edits.find: featuring a customized NGINX direct delivery configuration and an Ultrafast PHP implementation designed to process dynamic scripts up to 30% faster than vanilla PHP-FPM.
edits.replace: and on its GrowBig and GoGeek plans advertises what it calls "30% faster PHP" (a vendor claim we have not verified).
edits.reason: Attributed performance claim to vendor

edits.find: Their proprietary SuperCacher technology offers three tiers of performance enhancement: static asset caching, dynamic full-page caching, and Memcached database query acceleration. SiteGround also maintains rigorous security protocols, including custom web application firewall (WAF) rules updated daily and automated staging tools that simplify staging deployments.
edits.replace: SiteGround describes its caching as multilevel caching, managed through its Speed Optimizer WordPress plugin, and also markets security features and staging tools.
edits.reason: Removed unverified/outdated product details

edits.find: such as DigitalOcean, Linode, AWS, or Google Cloud. You maintain 100% dedicated access

edits.find: The platform runs an optimized software stack dubbed "ThunderStack," integrating NGINX as a reverse proxy, Apache for .htaccess compatibility, Varnish Cache for lightning-fast full-page caching, and Redis or Memcached for persistent database object caching.
edits.replace: The platform provides a managed server stack with built-in caching, and its pricing page lists Redis object caching on its plans.

edits.find: According to Google Web Vitals guidance, a TTFB under 800 milliseconds is considered acceptable for dynamic generation, but industry performance leaders aim for under 200 milliseconds on static cached requests. Deploying edge caching with a high-performance host frequently brings global TTFB down to 50ms–150ms.
edits.replace: Google's web.dev guidance suggests that, as a rough guide, most sites should aim for a TTFB of 0.8 seconds or less, and notes that TTFB is not a Core Web Vital. Cached pages served from a nearby edge location are typically much faster than uncached, dynamically generated pages.
edits.reason: Replaced unsourced figures with verified Google guidance

edits.find: While the minimum requirement for WordPress core is 64MB, modern themes and essential SEO/security plugin suites typically require at least 256MB of PHP memory allocation. For WooCommerce stores or advanced membership plugins, 512MB of PHP memory is strongly recommended to prevent memory exhaustion fatal errors during high-concurrency checkout runs.
edits.replace: WordPress itself runs within a modest PHP memory limit, but page builders, large plugin stacks, WooCommerce stores, and membership plugins need more. If you see "allowed memory size exhausted" errors, ask your host to raise the PHP memory limit or move to a plan that allows it.
edits.reason: Removed inaccurate/unsourced memory figures
